L169: ## MMR vaccine coverage for kindergarteners by school year (2009–2026)
L170: The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is very safe and effective. When more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated (coverage >95%), most people are protected through community immunity (herd immunity). However, cite25†vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners has decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in the 2025–2026 school year, leaving approximately 280,000 kindergartners at risk during the 2025–2026 school year.
L171: To dive into vaccine coverage data for MMR, visit cite26†VaxView .
L172: At local levels, vaccine coverage rates may vary considerably, and pockets of unvaccinated people can exist in states with high vaccination coverage. When measles gets into communities of unvaccinated people in the United States, outbreaks can occur.
L173: ## What to know about measles cases & outbreak data
L174: ### How does CDC collect and report data on measles cases and outbreaks?
L175: 
L176: State, local, tribal, and territorial health departments lead measles case and outbreak investigations. States notify CDC of measles cases reported in their jurisdictions and may request appropriate assistance from CDC to help with their investigations.
L177: 
L178: On this page CDC publishes:
L179:   * National measles case counts, including the total number of measles cases reported among international visitors to the United States. Cases are assigned to a year based on the epidemiological week of the date of rash onset. For example, cases with a rash onset date occurring during the last epidemiological week of 2025 (December 28, 2025, through January 3, 2026) are included in the 2025 case counts.
L180:   * Demographic and clinical data using the national total.
L181:   * The number of confirmed measles cases among U.S. residents in each jurisdiction.
L182:   * The cumulative number of measles outbreaks (defined as 3 or more related cases) that have occurred this year in the United States.
L183: ### Why do state case counts on this webpage differ from the numbers posted on state health department websites?
L184: State jurisdictions and CDC publicly report measles cases on their respective websites on different schedules. CDC is aware of probable measles cases being reported by jurisdictions, but updates on this webpage reflect only confirmed measles cases notified to CDC as of noon on Thursdays. States may report three or more linked cases in their state as an outbreak, but CDC may not report it as a distinct outbreak if these cases are associated with a previously reported outbreak.
L185: ### Why is there more measles activity?
L186:   * Measles was cite27†declared eliminated in the United States in 2000 . This was thanks to a very high percentage of people receiving the safe and effective measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. In recent years, however:
L187:   * cite28†U.S. national MMR coverage among kindergarteners has decreased and is now below the 95% coverage target—with much lower coverage in some communities.
L188:   * cite29†Global measles activity is increasing, meaning more chances of an unvaccinated person infected with measles abroad returning to the United States.
L189:   * Measles is not a seasonal virus. However, measles is often spread over times of high travel (like spring break, summer, or during holidays) or in situations where unvaccinated persons are in close quarters (like summer camp).
L190: Keep Reading cite27†History of Measles L191: ### Where are there current outbreaks of measles in the United States?
L192: 
L193: CDC publishes the cumulative number of measles outbreaks, defined as 3 or more related cases, that have occurred in the United States. Some states may have had multiple measles outbreaks, and a single reported multistate outbreak may have related cases reported in several states. States have the most up-to-date information about cases and ongoing outbreaks in their jurisdictions.
L194: ### How do measles outbreaks happen in the United States?
L195: 
L196: Measles is very contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. You can get measles just by being in a room where a person with measles has been. While measles has been eliminated in the United States since 2000, it is still common in many parts of the world.
L197: Every year, measles is brought into the United States by travelers who get measles while they are in other countries. Travelers who are infected with measles can bring it back to the United States and spread it to other people who are not protected. These travelers are usually unvaccinated U.S. residents who travel internationally. Far less frequently, they are international visitors. Few cases this year have been reported among international visitors.
L198: A measles outbreak is defined as 3 or more related cases. Most outbreaks in the United States are small, comprised of 6 people or fewer, usually within a household. When measles gets into a community that has lower vaccination rates it can spread quickly, causing larger outbreaks.
L199: 
L200: Keep Reading cite8†Plan for Travel L201: ### Why are some vaccinated people getting measles?
L202: Two doses of MMR vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles, 1 dose is 93% effective. It is uncommon for someone who is vaccinated to develop measles. However, breakthrough infections (when someone becomes infected after they have been vaccinated) can occur, especially in communities experiencing an outbreak where high levels of measles virus are circulating. The number of breakthrough infections is consistent with what we have seen in previous years (approximately 10% of all measles infections).
L203: ### How does CDC assess measles outbreak risk?
L204: 
L205: CDC is creating models to show how measles outbreaks could occur and spread in the United States. These models can be used to help health departments better identify communities at highest risk and manage healthcare resources.
L206: 
L207: Keep Reading cite30†Measles Outbreak Simulator L208: ### Why does CDC combine data on cases reported in people with 'unvaccinated' or 'unknown' MMR vaccination status?
L209: 
L210: The purpose of this webpage is to provide timely information to the public about confirmed measles cases in the United States. The data presented on this page show the portion of reported measles cases in people that lacked documentation of measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination and cases in people who had documentation of MMR vaccination, and the number of doses they received.
L211: Jurisdictions investigating measles cases assign 'unvaccinated' status to people with no record of MMR vaccination in the state's immunization registry. 'Unknown' vaccination status is assigned to people for whom immunization history or information is unavailable. Some jurisdictions initially report confirmed cases in these two categories combined, to more efficiently estimate the portion of the population that may not have immunity to measles.
L212: CDC receives reports of confirmed measles cases from state, territorial, and other public health departments. When CDC compiles confirmed cases to publish on this page, it combines the cases in people with 'unvaccinated' status and 'unknown' vaccination status into one category. When CDC publishes detailed reports and summaries, it publishes data on unvaccinated and unknown categories separately.
L213: 
L214: Keep Reading cite31†Measles Update — United States, January 1–April 17, 2025 L215: ### How serious is measles?
L216: 
L217: Measles is an extremely infectious, and potentially severe rash illness. cite27†Before the measles vaccine was introduced, an estimated 48,000 people were hospitalized and 400–500 people died in the United States each year.
L218: 
L219: Keep Reading cite4†Measles Symptoms and Complications L220: ### How do I protect myself?
L221: 
L222: The best way to protect yourself against measles is with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Talk to your healthcare provider about vaccination, cite8†especially if planning to travel .
L223: 
L224: Keep Reading cite7†Measles Vaccination L225: ## History of measles cases
L226: 
L227: Measles was cite27†officially eliminated from the United States in 2000 , meaning there is no measles spreading within the country and new cases are only found when someone contracts measles abroad and returns to the country. Achieving measles elimination status in the United States was a historic public health achievement. The below figure illustrates how common measles was before vaccines and how vaccine policy enabled elimination.

Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. # Measles Cases and Outbreaks For Everyone [Sept. 18, 2026, visit link for details.](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/#content-sources) [Español](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/es/data-research/index.html) ## What to know - Updated on September 18, 2026. - The data on this page reflect confirmed measles cases reported to CDC as of 12:00PM on Thursday. ![Map of airplanes traveling across the world.](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/media/images/2025/12/Measles-World-Map-Travel_update_9.12B-gradient.jpg) ## Measles cases in 2026 ### **Resources for Communities with a Measles Outbreak:** - [Sample Community Letter About Measles](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/media/files/2025/05/measles-toolkit-sample-community-letter.docx) - [Be Ready for Measles Toolkit](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/php/toolkit/index.html) - [There's a Current Outbreak of Measles](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/downloads/measles-factsheet-outbreak-508.pdf) - [Do You Think Your Child Has Measles?](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/downloads/measles-factsheet-seek-care-508.pdf) As of September 17, 2026, 3,471 confirmed\* measles cases were reported in the United States in 2026. Among these, 3,454 measles cases were reported by 47 jurisdictions: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York City, New York State, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming. A total of 17 measles cases were reported among international visitors to the United States. There have been 39 new outbreaks\*\* reported in 2026, and 95% of confirmed cases (3,296 of 3,471) are outbreak-associated (1,920 from outbreaks starting in 2026 and 1,376 from outbreaks that started in 2025). For the full year of 2025, a total of 2,289 confirmed\* measles cases were reported in the United States. Among these, 2,263 measles cases were reported by 45 jurisdictions: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York City, New York State, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and Wyoming. A total of 26 measles cases were reported among international visitors to the United States. There were 48 outbreaks\*\* reported in 2025, and 90% of confirmed cases (2,066 of 2,289) were outbreak-associated. For comparison, 16 outbreaks were reported during 2024 and 69% of cases (198 of 285) were outbreak-associated. \*CDC is aware of probable measles cases being reported by jurisdictions. Estimates shown for these states are the percentage of kindergartners who received all doses of all vaccines required for school entry. ## What to know about measles cases & outbreak data [Expand All](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/#) ### How does CDC collect and report data on measles cases and outbreaks? State, local, tribal, and territorial health departments lead measles case and outbreak investigations. States notify CDC of measles cases reported in their jurisdictions and may request appropriate assistance from CDC to help with their investigations. On this page CDC publishes: - National measles case counts, including the total number of measles cases reported among international visitors to the United States. Cases are assigned to a year based on the epidemiological week of the date of rash onset. For example, cases with a rash onset date occurring during the last epidemiological week of 2025 (December 28, 2025, through January 3, 2026) are included in the 2025 case counts. - Demographic and clinical data using the national total. - The number of confirmed measles cases among U.S. residents in each jurisdiction. - The cumulative number of measles outbreaks (defined as 3 or more related cases) that have occurred this year in the United States. ### Why do state case counts on this webpage differ from the numbers posted on state health department websites? State jurisdictions and CDC publicly report measles cases on their respective websites on different schedules. CDC is aware of probable measles cases being reported by jurisdictions, but updates on this webpage reflect only confirmed measles cases notified to CDC as of noon on Thursdays. States may report three or more linked cases in their state as an outbreak, but CDC may not report it as a distinct outbreak if these cases are associated with a previously reported outbreak. ### Why is there more measles activity? - Measles was [declared eliminated in the United States in 2000](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html). This was thanks to a very high percentage of people receiving the safe and effective measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. In recent years, however: - [U.S. national MMR coverage among kindergarteners](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/wr/mm7341a3.htm) has decreased and is now below the 95% coverage target—with much lower coverage in some communities. - [Global measles activity](https://www.cdc.gov/globalhealth/measles/index.html) is increasing, meaning more chances of an unvaccinated person infected with measles abroad returning to the United States. - Measles is not a seasonal virus. However, measles is often spread over times of high travel (like spring break, summer, or during holidays) or in situations where unvaccinated persons are in close quarters (like summer camp). **Keep Reading** [History of Measles](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html) ### Where are there current outbreaks of measles in the United States? CDC publishes the cumulative number of measles outbreaks, defined as 3 or more related cases, that have occurred in the United States. Some states may have had multiple measles outbreaks, and a single reported multistate outbreak may have related cases reported in several states. States have the most up-to-date information about cases and ongoing outbreaks in their jurisdictions. ### How do measles outbreaks happen in the United States? Measles is very contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. You can get measles just by being in a room where a person with measles has been. While measles has been eliminated in the United States since 2000, it is still common in many parts of the world. Every year, measles is brought into the United States by travelers who get measles while they are in other countries. Travelers who are infected with measles can bring it back to the United States and spread it to other people who are not protected. These travelers are usually unvaccinated U.S. residents who travel internationally. Far less frequently, they are international visitors. Few cases this year have been reported among international visitors. A measles outbreak is defined as 3 or more related cases. Most outbreaks in the United States are small, comprised of 6 people or fewer, usually within a household. When measles gets into a community that has lower vaccination rates it can spread quickly, causing larger outbreaks. **Keep Reading** [Plan for Travel](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/travel/index.html) ### Why are some vaccinated people getting measles? Two doses of MMR vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles, 1 dose is 93% effective. It is uncommon for someone who is vaccinated to develop measles. However, breakthrough infections (when someone becomes infected after they have been vaccinated) can occur, especially in communities experiencing an outbreak where high levels of measles virus are circulating. The number of breakthrough infections is consistent with what we have seen in previous years (approximately 10% of all measles infections). ### How does CDC assess measles outbreak risk? CDC is creating models to show how measles outbreaks could occur and spread in the United States. These models can be used to help health departments better identify communities at highest risk and manage healthcare resources. **Keep Reading** [Measles Outbreak Simulator](https://www.cdc.gov/cfa-modeling-and-forecasting/measles-outbreak-simulator/index.html) ### Why does CDC combine data on cases reported in people with 'unvaccinated' or 'unknown' MMR vaccination status? The purpose of this webpage is to provide timely information to the public about confirmed measles cases in the United States. The data presented on this page show the portion of reported measles cases in people that lacked documentation of measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination and cases in people who had documentation of MMR vaccination, and the number of doses they received. Jurisdictions investigating measles cases assign 'unvaccinated' status to people with no record of MMR vaccination in the state's immunization registry. 'Unknown' vaccination status is assigned to people for whom immunization history or information is unavailable. Some jurisdictions initially report confirmed cases in these two categories combined, to more efficiently estimate the portion of the population that may not have immunity to measles. CDC receives reports of confirmed measles cases from state, territorial, and other public health departments. When CDC compiles confirmed cases to publish on this page, it combines the cases in people with 'unvaccinated' status and 'unknown' vaccination status into one category. When CDC publishes detailed reports and summaries, it publishes data on unvaccinated and unknown categories separately. **Keep Reading** [Measles Update — United States, January 1–April 17, 2025](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/wr/mm7414a1.htm) ### How serious is measles? Measles is an extremely infectious, and potentially severe rash illness. [Before the measles vaccine](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html) was introduced, an estimated 48,000 people were hospitalized and 400–500 people died in the United States each year. **Keep Reading** [Measles Symptoms and Complications](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/signs-symptoms/index.html) ### How do I protect myself? The best way to protect yourself against measles is with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Talk to your healthcare provider about vaccination, [especially if planning to travel](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/travel/index.html). **Keep Reading** [Measles Vaccination](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/vaccines/index.html) ## History of measles cases Measles was [officially eliminated from the United States in 2000](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html), meaning there is no measles spreading within the country and new cases are only found when someone contracts measles abroad and returns to the country.
